title: Let’s Fix the Cause, Not Just the Symptom
scene: The same small problem keeps coming back at work. Instead of applying another quick fix, you want to understand the cause and prevent the issue from happening again.
sceneJa: 同じ小さな問題が仕事で何度も再発している場面。その都度応急処置をするのではなく、原因を特定して再発を防ぎたいと考えている。

chunks.en: We could fix this one issue now
chunks.ja: この問題だけなら今直せます
ただ、気になっているのは
何度も再発することです

chunks.en: Before we make another quick fix,
chunks.ja: また応急的に直す前に
何がそれを引き起こしているのか

chunks.en: It might take a little longer today,
chunks.ja: 今日は少し余計に時間がかかるかもしれません
でも、それによって避けられるかもしれません
対応しなければならなくなることを

chunks.en: the same thing again next week.
If we can identify the root cause,
chunks.ja: 根本原因を特定できれば
それが再び起きることを

questions.question: Which chunking is most natural?
options: It might take a little longer today / but it could save us / from having to deal with / the same thing again next week
It might take / a little longer today but / it could save / us from having to deal with the same thing again next week
It might / take a little / longer today but it could / save us from having to deal
questions.explanation: The first version keeps the contrast, the verb phrase ‘save us’, and the complement ‘from having to deal with ...’ in natural meaning groups.

questions.question: What does ‘in the first place’ mean here?
questions.explanation: ‘In the first place’ means ‘to begin with’ or ‘originally’. Here it asks what is causing the problem at its source.

questions.question: Why does the speaker want to identify the root cause?
options: To write a more detailed report
To prevent the same problem from happening again
questions.explanation: The speaker wants to move beyond repeated quick fixes and stop the issue from recurring.

speak: Sound thoughtful rather than frustrated. Start ‘We could fix this one issue now’ lightly, slow down at ‘will keep coming back’, and give a little emphasis to ‘the root cause’ and ‘prevent it from happening again’. The tone should suggest a practical long-term solution, not criticism.
review: Previous session: check the wider impact before agreeing to a small change. Useful chunks were ‘what else it might affect’, ‘trace it through’, and ‘If the impact is limited, ...’. Today goes one step further: instead of asking only what a change affects, ask why the problem is happening in the first place. The flow is quick fix → recurring problem → root cause → prevention.
